name: IDRA-21

card.summary: A research AMPA-receptor modulator studied in animals for memory and learning, which is why it appears in nootropic circles aiming for sharper focus and recall.
card.note: Research chemical with no human trials; animal work reports increased neuron injury after ischemia.

quick.overview:
IDRA-21 is a benzothiadiazine compound that positively modulates AMPA-type glutamate receptors. Fidia Farmaceutici in Italy investigated it in the 1990s as a possible treatment for memory problems, and it has remained a research tool.

In animal studies it improved performance on memory and learning tasks in monkeys, at oral doses reported to be far lower than those of the related compound aniracetam. Community interest comes from this cognitive-enhancement research.
quick.mechanism: It slows the desensitization and deactivation of AMPA receptors, so excitatory glutamate signals last longer and are stronger. Lab work also found it reduces NMDA-receptor currents in cultured neurons, and that it influences long-term potentiation, a cellular correlate of learning.
quick.risks: No human clinical data have been reported. In rats, doses given orally increased hippocampal neuron loss after induced ischemia, and the authors noted that AMPA potentiation could matter in conditions such as stroke or seizures. It is not an approved medicine.

chain: Stronger excitatory signalling in memory circuits
Sharper memory and focus for work and study (claimed)
angle.text: IDRA-21 is discussed by people who want sharper memory and focus, a route to better performance rather than to a direct change in appearance. The memory effects reported are from monkey and cell studies, and no human data exist.

lead: IDRA-21 (7-chloro-3-methyl-3,4-dihydro-2H-1,2,4-benzothiadiazine S,S-dioxide) is a synthetic positive allosteric modulator of AMPA glutamate receptors, studied as a cognitive enhancer [1][2]. People interested in it hope for better memory and mental sharpness, which supports performance in work and study and, for those in appearance-focused communities, the broader goal of operating at a higher level.

It reduces AMPA receptor desensitization, prolonging excitatory synaptic currents [3][4]. In monkeys it improved delayed-matching and visual recognition memory tasks [5][6] and reversed learning impairment induced by alprazolam [7]. A review of the compound class describes AMPA modulators as potential treatments for conditions with impaired memory, while noting the excitotoxicity risk of overactivating the receptor [2].

It was developed by Fidia Farmaceutici in Italy in the 1990s; development was reported discontinued in 2003, and no human clinical data have been reported [1]. It is a research chemical, not an approved medicine.

paras: IDRA-21 is a small molecule of the benzothiadiazine class, with molecular formula C8H9ClN2O2S [1]. It is a structural relative of the diuretic and vasodilator diazoxide and of cyclothiazide, a compound used in laboratories to block AMPA receptor desensitization, and it is described as a congener of aniracetam, a nootropic of the racetam family [7][1]. The molecule has a chiral center; Grokipedia says that only one mirror-image form is behaviorally active, a point reported from rat studies and an enantiomer-separation paper [1][12]. A later group of 5'-alkyl benzothiadiazides was made to produce modulators with improved affinity [13].

AMPA receptors carry most fast excitatory signalling in the brain and are central to the synaptic strengthening that underlies learning. After glutamate binds, they normally close quickly, a process called desensitization. IDRA-21 binds at an allosteric site and slows this closing, so each synaptic event lasts longer and carries more charge [2][1]. Structural work on the GluR2 receptor has mapped the thiazide binding site where compounds of this type sit [9], and thermodynamic studies compare how different modulators bind [14].

The compound is described as a partial modulator. In rat cerebellar granule neurons, it showed lower intrinsic activity than cyclothiazide, produced shorter calcium transients, and was not neurotoxic in that preparation up to 100 micromolar, whereas cyclothiazide was strongly neurotoxic at much lower concentrations [3]. In cultured cerebellar cells IDRA-21 also inhibited synaptic and extrasynaptic NMDA receptor events, with larger effects on NR2B-containing receptors [4]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, adds that it modestly augments GABA currents and acts on kainate receptors [1].

The best-known work is in primates. In young and aged rhesus monkeys, IDRA-21 improved accuracy in delayed matching-to-sample tasks [5]. In young macaques, a visual recognition memory study compared it with huperzine A, a cholinesterase inhibitor, in animals that were presumably already performing near their best [6]. In patas monkeys, IDRA-21 and aniracetam each attenuated alprazolam-induced learning deficits in a complex repeated-acquisition task, with IDRA-21 reported as potent in that setting [7]. Rodent hippocampal slice work found that its effect on long-term potentiation, a cellular model of memory, depended on conditions [8].
A 1998 review placed AMPA receptor modulation among strategies for neurological disease and noted that overactivation of these receptors is implicated in seizures and ischemic damage [2].

Reviews note that excessive AMPA activation can cause excitotoxicity, as in seizures or ischemia [2]. In a 1998 study, oral IDRA-21 increased CA1 hippocampal neuron loss after global ischemia in rats, and killed cultured hippocampal neurons in the presence of glutamate through AMPA receptor activation; the authors concluded that drugs potentiating AMPA receptors would need careful consideration in conditions such as stroke and seizures [10]. The same group of compounds can behave differently in other preparations, where IDRA-21 was not neurotoxic [3]. No human safety data are available.

Fidia Farmaceutici investigated IDRA-21 in the 1990s for memory impairments linked to aging, drug-induced deficits and ischemia; the program was reported discontinued in 2003 [1]. Key early papers appeared in 1995-1997 [7][3].

IDRA-21 is a research compound sold online for laboratory use and discussed in nootropic communities as a more potent relative of the racetams and aniracetam-like compounds, a framing that follows from the animal data [7][1]. It belongs to the broader ampakine family of AMPA modulators, which includes CX546 and others studied in labs [15]. Because no human trial has been published, accounts of use in people are anecdotal, and this wiki does not give dosing or sourcing information.

No studies found in humans. The relevant research is in animals and cells: IDRA-21 improved delayed-matching performance in young and aged rhesus monkeys [5], enhanced visual recognition memory in young macaques [6], and abated alprazolam-induced cognitive impairment in patas monkeys [7]. In hippocampal slices it affected long-term potentiation [8]. A related review of modulators of excitatory neurotransmission discusses their potential for neurological disease without human trials of this compound [2].
